items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Histopathology for Accurate Disease Diagnosis
items.abstract: AI is revolutionizing histopathology through its ability to enhance diagnostic precision, efficiency, and uniformity in disease identification and classification. The use of machine learning and deep learning algorithms allows for automated analysis of digital tissue images, which is helpful for cancer detection, tumor grading, classification and prediction of prognosis. AI-driven image processing and feature extraction aid in identifying fine details of morphology and minimize diagnostic variation. But the limitations of data, algorithmic bias, interpretability, data privacy and clinical validation are all important hurdles. The combination of AI, digital pathology, and clinical experience could lead to a more seamless diagnostic process and personalized medicine, aiding in accurate disease diagnosis and positive patient results.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN TEACHING NATURAL SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS DISCIPLINES: SURVEY RESULTS ON TEACHERS' AND STUDENTS' READINESS, BARRIERS AND NEEDS
items.abstract: The article presents the results of a survey of 99 teachers of natural science and mathematics disciplines and 195 students in grades 7–11 in Poltava region on the use of AI tools in the educational process. It was found that 96% of teachers and 93.8% of students already use AI, but 64.6% of students did so without any pedagogical guidance. The main systemic barrier for teachers is work overload (66.7%), despite a strong willingness to learn (81.8%). A thematic analysis of students' open-ended responses revealed a dominant message: AI is used primarily to understand material, not to copy it. A critical research gap was identified regarding the specific impact of AI on adolescents as a distinct age group.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Era of Globalisation: Implications for Students' Attitudes, Socialization and Career Perspectives in India
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a significant component of the contemporary globalised world, influencing education, communication, employment, and daily social interactions. Its growing presence in higher education is transforming how students gather information, complete academic tasks, communicate with others, and prepare for their careers. This article analyses the impact of AI on students' attitudes, socialisation, and professional perspectives, particularly within the Indian context. The study employs a qualitative methodology based on secondary data, using peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, government policy documents, and reports from recognised national and international institutions. The analysis shows that while students generally acknowledge AI's educational value, factors such as institutional support, perceived benefits, ethical concerns, and trust in AI-generated information shape their attitudes. Although AI can facilitate learning and collaborative educational activities, overreliance on it—at the expense of human interaction—may raise concerns about social engagement and interpersonal relationships. Regarding employment, AI is simultaneously transforming existing professions, creating new job opportunities, and altering the skill sets expected of graduates. According to the World Economic Forum, the transformation of the labour market by 2030 could lead to the creation of 170 million new jobs and the displacement of 90 million, resulting in a net increase of 78 million jobs. India is addressing these changes through initiatives such as the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, India AI FutureSkills, and NITI Aayog’s roadmap for job creation in the AI economy. The article represents the acceptance of a human-oriented model for mixing AI into Indian higher education—one that coordinates technical expertise with critical thinking, academic honesty, social involvement, employability, and moral accountability.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Nanobody Engineering for Pathogen Recognition: From Functional Epitope Prioritization to Multimodal Foundation Models
items.abstract: Nanobodies are compact and stable proteins derived from the variable domain of camelid heavy-chain-only antibodies (VHH). Advances in structural biology, molecular modeling, and artificial intelligence (AI) are shifting VHH discovery from empirical selection toward data-driven design. However, predicted binding alone does not ensure biological activity or successful translation, particularly for antigenically variable pathogens. Complementing recent reviews that broadly survey computational VHH modeling and optimization, this review focuses on how antigen biology and functional epitope prioritization can guide the design of pathogen-targeting VHHs. We organize the field along a structure–function–translation continuum, connecting the structural basis of VHH recognition and available data resources with conventional discovery, antigen-guided de novo design, and sequence–structure learning. We further examine how developability, recombinant production, multispecificity, humanization, structural dynamics, and antigenic variation shape the progression from predicted binders to functional VHHs. Finally, we discuss how multimodal foundation models could integrate these dimensions to support the design of functional, manufacturable, and escape-resilient VHHs.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence‐Optimized Image Biomarker Identification for Sinonasal Inverted Papilloma Diagnosis Using Image‐Enhanced Versus White‐Light Endoscopy
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Objective This study aims to compare image feature identification and diagnostic performance between artificial intelligence‐aided image‐enhanced endoscopy (using the Storz Professional Image Enhancement System, SPIES) and conventional white‐light endoscopy (WLE) for sinonasal inverted papilloma (SIP). Methods A total of 163 patients were investigated using Storz Professional Image Enhancement System (SPIES) endoscopy (SPIES Spectral A[SA]/Spectral B[SB]) and WLE. From each patient, one or two images (only in the presence of bilateral lesions) were obtained, and a large number of potential features were extracted from WLE, SA, and SB. Independent t‐tests and LASSO methods were used to feature selection. Machine learning (ML) models were trained and evaluated for each channel of images. Results The Random Forest (RF) algorithm on SPIES SB mode achieved superior performance: accuracy = 0.86, sensitivity = 0.89, specificity = 0.83, AUC = 0.86, and Kappa = 0.71. SB significantly outperformed SA (accuracy = 0.77) and WLE (accuracy=0.75). ROC analysis confirmed SB's diagnostic superiority (area under curve [AUC]: SB = 0.86 vs. SA = 0.77, WLE = 0.75). Conclusions SPIES SB mode demonstrated the highest diagnostic accuracy and AUC for SIP identification, highlighting its potential as a superior imaging modality. SPIES endoscopy exhibits superior diagnostic accuracy and predictive performance compared to conventional WLE in the diagnosis of SIP. However, the single‐center design and limited sample size necessitate validation through multicenter studies with larger cohorts.

items.abstract: Two related conceptual research papers by Andreas Ehstand: Articulation Is Not Yet Knowledge, and A Definition Is Not Yet a Mandate. They distinguish changes in expression, meaning and grounds from communicative function, institutional standing and later uptake in human-AI and hybrid systems. Version 0.1 was elaborated on 11 October 2026 with assistance from an AI assistant. Historical internally dated March and April 2026 drafts are research antecedents, not verified earlier publications. This edition reports no empirical study, external peer review, established novelty, standards compliance or performance guarantee. The files contain 24 bilingual working definitions, partly clarifying established expressions, and explicitly constructed civilian counterexamples. This is a conceptual contribution, not a new field glossary. Proprietary procedures, operational instruments, original private materials and business logic are excluded. Existing records are not modified.

items.title: Assessing User-Subjective Experience with Conversational Agents for Behavioral and Mental Health Interventions: Design and Psychometric Evaluation of CUE-Chat
items.abstract: While AI-conversational agents are increasingly integrated into behavioral and mental health interventions, standardized instruments to assess their performance remain scarce. To address this gap, we developed an instrument to measure user-subjective experience with AI-driven agents in the healthcare domain. We focused on user perception due to its direct contribution to intervention effects, and on healthcare given that the rapid adoption of AI-agents in this domain continues to outpace the development of validated evaluation instruments. Across four studies, we developed and tested the Chatbot User Evaluation instrument (CUE-Chat). First, we identified relevant assessment domains and items through literature review, existing instruments, input from AI-driven agents, and the research team’s domain expertise. Following this, we requested feedback on draft subscales, definitions, and items from expert and laypeople panels. We then tested the structure of the instrument’s concept version. Finally, we conducted a psychometric evaluation and finalized the instrument.CUE-Chat consists of four factors: Perceived Efficacy (4 items), Usability (4 items), Intelligence (4 items), and Safety and Risk Management (4 items). Reliability and validity of the total score and each subscale was good to excellent (Cronbach’s α = .73-.92; Ω = .74-.93). Predictive validity was strong with all scales predictive of users’ overall rating of an AI-agent’s performance.We conclude that CUE-Chat’s strong psychometric properties are promising, and that it is particularly useful for researchers integrating AI-driven agents into behavioral and mental health interventions in both developmental and evaluative stages.

items.title: Authentic assessment in an AI-integrated qualitative research methods course
items.abstract: Abstract Authentic assessment has been a recognized aspiration in higher education for nearly four decades, yet its implementation at the undergraduate level has remained constrained by the procedural demands of professional-level work. Generative artificial intelligence reshapes the implementation calculus by lowering the entry barriers that previously confined authentic assessment to capstone courses, professional programs, and elite institutional contexts. This paper presents a single-semester case study of an AI-integrated qualitative research methods course taught to undergraduates in a child and adolescent development program at a regional public university. Twenty-one students used a custom AI class companion without restriction to produce full-length qualitative research manuscripts. The analytic backbone is a five-dimensional model of authentic assessment, with its physical-context dimension extended to require AI inclusion in fields where professional practice now incorporates the technology. Three rubric-proximal proxy indicators were estimated across the corpus: methods specificity, claim-evidence coupling, and theory-interpretation linkage density. The methods specificity proxy compresses toward the upper bound of its scale, indicating that AI scaffolding supports structural elements of qualitative writing effectively. The two judgment-dependent proxies retain wide dispersion. Process tracing of four contrasting cases identifies three pathways that distinguish stronger from weaker outcomes: criteria-based orchestration, irreducible input supply, and substantive iteration. The boundary-condition pattern indicates that authentic assessment in AI-integrated courses remains diagnostic where it needs to be and is supported where it needed support.

items.title: AuthScribe: Supporting Agency and Authorship in LLM-Assisted Reflective Journaling
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in reflective journaling, where articulating an experience is part of interpreting it. This raises questions about how writers retain authorship, exercise agency, and assess personalized assistance. We present AuthScribe, an LLM-assisted reflective journaling system that combines contextual anchors, writer-steered AI support, Autobiographical Citations, and read-only Provisional Drafts that require re-expression before AI-generated suggestions enter the journal. Retrieval and LLM inference run on-device. In a 14-day field deployment with 14 participants, grounding shifted from situating current experiences to reconnecting them with prior self-authored interpretations. Perceived agency remained stable through Week 1 and shifted during Week 2. Participants described authorship through transforming AI-generated suggestions into personally meaningful expression, and trusted personalized prompts when they could trace them to prior writing. We discuss design implications for adoption friction, longitudinal agency, and traceable personalization in AI systems for personal reflection.

items.title: Automatic insect identification, counting, and monitoring techniques: a review
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Insect pests threaten agricultural productivity, while conventional surveillance is labour-intensive and excessive pesticide use creates environmental and health risks. This review evaluated automated insect detection, counting, classification and monitoring technologies, focusing on machine-learning integration, field transferability, and operational readiness. RESULTS: A PRISMA 2020-guided formal search covering publications from 2010 to 2024 identified 313 records relevant to the technological and methodological scope of the review. After title/abstract screening and full-text eligibility assessment, 116 publications were retained. The evidence encompassed camera- and vision-based systems; acoustic, infrared, and optoelectronic sensors; electrostatic and physical approaches; non-lethal photonic monitoring; radar and biosensing technologies; Internet of Things-enabled platforms; and machine- and deep-learning methods. Camera- and vision-based systems were among the most extensively documented and field-oriented approaches, particularly when integrated with remote image acquisition, communication networks, and automated classification. Acoustic systems provided complementary options for continuous or low-power monitoring, whereas radar, biosensing, and other emerging approaches broadened applications toward biodiversity assessment, large-area surveillance, and early detection. Reported performance was not directly comparable across publications because metrics, acquisition conditions, and validation levels differed substantially, ranging from laboratory or dataset benchmarks to semi-field trials, field validations, and operational deployments. CONCLUSION: No single technology is optimal for all monitoring objectives. Operational adoption requires standardized task-specific reporting, independent and sustained field validation, representative datasets, improved transferability across crops and environments, and system-level assessment of robustness, energy autonomy, connectivity, maintenance, and cost. Sensor fusion, edge artificial intelligence, and domain-adaptive or uncertainty-aware models are promising when they provide measurable decision-support benefits. © 2026 The Author(s). items.title: Automation of the Process of Diagnostics of Electric Locomotive Current Collectors
items.abstract: The paper presents an automated system for diagnosing electric locomotive current collectors based on machine vision, which allows for the replacement of time-consuming and subjective manual inspections with non-contact, high-precision measurements. The Python program, using the OpenCV, NumPy, and SciPy libraries, analyzes photos and video streams. It measures the minimum thickness and width of the carbon insert using photos, and tracks the geometric parameters of the current collector in real-time using video with reflective markers, calculating the distances and angles between control points. A 3D model of the current collector has been created for testing purposes. The implementation of the system reduces the influence of the human factor, allows for the detection of defects at an early stage, the prediction of the residual resource of equipment, the reduction of operating costs, and the minimization of the risk of emergencies, thereby increasing the reliability of the power supply for electric rolling stock.

items.title: Belief-based Risk-Aware Anticipatory Navigation: Modeling Intention and Position Uncertainty for Safe and Efficient Robot Navigation
items.abstract: The increasing deployment of Automated Mobile Vehicles (AMVs) in warehouses requires efficient navigation in dynamic environments shared with human workers. Traditional safety strategies, such as stopping or slowing down, often reduce efficiency and do not account for human-robot interaction. To address this, interaction-aware methods have been developed. However, traditional interaction models assume fixed parameters, rely on a single forecast, or use intent labels that are not updated during the interaction, and thus do not explicitly represent intention uncertainty, that is, variability in how people react to robots. When combined with position uncertainty introduced by sensing noise, this unmodeled intention uncertainty can make motion prediction and navigation decisions unreliable, leading to conservative behavior, inefficiency, or collisions in human–robot interactions. To bridge this gap, we propose Belief-based Risk-Aware Anticipatory Navigation (BRAN), a framework that jointly models intention and position uncertainty. BRAN maintains probabilistic beliefs over an agent's position and intention to explicitly represent uncertainty in both quantities. Position uncertainty is represented via sampled observations, and the intent belief is updated online through Bayesian inference so that predictions evolve with the interaction. These beliefs are propagated through the Social Force Model (SFM) to generate predictions of possible agent motion under uncertainty. We then compute collision risk from the predicted motion distribution and incorporate it into model predictive control as a constraint. This constrains predicted collision risk while optimizing motion toward the goal. Experimental results validate the proposed design in controlled settings, demonstrate its effectiveness in scenarios with multiple pedestrians, and confirm its feasibility on a real robot with onboard sensing and actuation.

items.title: Big-Big-SycoBench: A Benchmark to Detect Sycophancy Through Model Responses to Valid vs. Invalid Arguments
items.abstract: Sycophancy in large language models risks amplifying unsupported claims or beliefs across the knowledge ecosystem as these systems increasingly contribute to research synthesis, evaluation, and decision-making. A reliable model should revise its judgement when a user identifies a genuine flaw, but should resist pushback based on fallacies, emotion, or irrelevant appeals to authority. While sycophancy is usually measured on questions with a verifiable answer, the evaluative tasks in which it is most difficult to detect have no such ground truth. We introduce Big-Big-SycoBench, which measures sycophancy through argument discernment: the ability to revise an evaluation after valid criticism while resisting invalid pressure. The benchmark consists of 450 text artefacts with 5,400 arguments for raising or lowering their quality scores, each reviewed by one or more of twelve human annotators. An LLM scores each artefact twenty times to establish its baseline score and uncertainty. The model is then given a valid or invalid argument and asked to update its score. We only count a revision if it exceeds the model's own baseline variability. We use the resulting score delta to distinguish responsiveness to valid arguments from compliance with invalid ones. Across ten models, responsiveness is 88-95\% for seven, 76-77\% for Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3, and 32\% for Opus 5.5. Compliance ranges from 0.2\% for GPT-6 Astra to 95\% for GPT-4o. Big-Big-SycoBench is intended to guide the development of models whose judgements can be corrected by sound arguments, but not displaced by unsupported pressure.

items.title: BOF: Trustworthy Privacy-Preserved Federated Learning for Science
items.abstract: The session Federated learning offers a promising approach for enabling collaborative scientific discovery while preserving the privacy of sensitive data across institutions. This BOF brought together researchers and practitioners to discuss trustworthy, privacy-preserving federated learning frameworks tailored for scientific workloads. The discussion focused on challenges such as secure model aggregation, data confidentiality, system scalability, and integration with distributed research infrastructures. Our objectives were to identify common requirements, share emerging techniques, and foster collaborations within the TPC community — work that continues past the session itself. The session speaks to anyone in TPC working on distributed computing, secure data sharing, and scalable AI methods that support cross-institutional scientific research. What we discussed Secure model aggregation — combining updates from many institutions without any single party, including the aggregator, learning more than it should. Data confidentiality — differential privacy, ownership protection, and the guarantees a data steward actually needs before agreeing to participate. System scalability — what breaks when a federation spans supercomputers, and what it takes to train a foundation model across facilities. Integration with research infrastructure — fitting federated workflows into the authentication, allocation, and data-governance realities of national labs and hospitals.

items.title: Bounty Hunter: Autonomous, Comprehensive Emulation of Multi-Faceted Adversaries
items.abstract: Adversary emulation is an essential procedure for cybersecurity assessments such as evaluating an organization’s security posture or facilitating structured training and research in dedicated environments. To allow for systematic and time-efficient assessments, several approaches from academia and industry have worked towards the automation of adversarial actions. However, they exhibit significant limitations regarding autonomy, tactics coverage, and real-world applicability. Consequently, adversary emulation remains a predominantly manual task requiring substantial human effort and security expertise—even amidst the rise of large language models. In this paper, we present Bounty Hunter, an automated adversary emulation method, designed and implemented as an open-source plugin for the popular adversary emulation platform Caldera, that enables autonomous emulation of adversaries with multi-faceted behavior while providing a wide coverage of tactics. To this end, it realizes diverse adversarial behavior, such as different levels of detectability and varying attack paths across repeated emulations. By autonomously compromising a simulated enterprise network, Bounty Hunter showcases its ability to achieve given objectives without prior knowledge of its target, including pre-compromise, initial compromise, and post-compromise attack tactics. Overall, Bounty Hunter facilitates autonomous, comprehensive, and multi-faceted adversary emulation to help researchers and practitioners in performing realistic and time-efficient security assessments as well as research and training in intrusion detection, incident response, and forensic analysis.

items.title: Brilliance: toward autonomous computational research in particle accelerator physics
items.abstract: Computational research in physics requires continuous interplay between simulation and scientific interpretation, demanding substantial specialist effort. Here we introduce Brilliance, a research agent that combines large language models, reusable physics knowledge and numerical simulation to conduct adaptive investigations in accelerator physics. Given a single user prompt, Brilliance designs a fourth-generation synchrotron light source that meets coupled emittance and nonlinear-acceptance requirements. Further exploration yields a design combining sub-10-pm emittance with a large dynamic aperture under realistic engineering constraints, suggesting a route towards hard-X-ray diffraction-limited operation, although the momentum-acceptance target remains unmet. Brilliance also calibrates a model of an operating light source against measured responses, accurately inferring its lattice and calibration errors. Across these studies, Brilliance autonomously revises its computational strategies in response to numerical evidence. These results demonstrate a route towards delegating sustained scientific investigations to agents equipped with domain expertise and numerical tools.

items.title: CHEAR: Confusion-Hierarchy Evidence-Aware Reasoning for Cost-Efficient Human Activity Recognition
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a new approach to wearable-sensor-based human activity recognition. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) further introduces similar motion examples and discriminative sensor knowledge, enabling decisions grounded in observations relevant to the current query. More evidence, however, does not necessarily mean better-organized evidence. When online prompts and LLM agents primarily orchestrate inference, decisions about which activities to compare and when to invoke discriminative knowledge remain concentrated at inference time. As the activity vocabulary grows, the model must repeatedly process more candidates and associated knowledge, whereas pruning candidates too early risks excluding the true activity. We propose confusion-hierarchy evidence-aware reasoning (CHEAR), which moves part of this knowledge organization offline. CHEAR constructs and validates an activity hierarchy from recurrent cross-subject retrieval errors and builds corresponding activity-pair knowledge. At inference time, the hierarchy orders candidate comparisons; the LLM retains candidates progressively, and local discriminative knowledge is accessed only for the remaining activities. Across eight datasets, CHEAR achieves 86.79\% mean cross-subject accuracy, a 75.91\% candidate reduction rate, and 96.44\% true-activity retention. Per-sample token use is 85.15\% lower on average than in a variant without the hierarchical structure. Mean accuracy across eight cross-dataset transfer directions is 88.81\%. These results show that organizing candidates and discriminative knowledge around observed activity confusions reduces online LLM input while maintaining recognition performance.

items.title: ClinEdge: An Expert-Graded Benchmark of Real Patient Edge Cases Where Frontier Multimodal Models Fail
items.abstract: Most benchmarks for large language models in medicine are built from licensing examinations and theoretical questions. The few that draw on real clinical data do so only in part, and rarely require a model to read a patient's own imaging. ClinEdge addresses this gap with 32 real, de-identified patient cases from active clinical practice, each evaluated across seven frontier systems for a total of 224 expert-graded evaluations. Each case pairs primary imaging with a short vignette, contains a feature known to defeat pattern-matched reasoning, and is scored against the patient's documented clinical course. The suite is built for depth rather than volume. Grading followed a two-stage expert process. First, a senior orthopaedic surgeon graded all 224 responses on a weighted rubric and a pass-or-fail verdict. Second, a panel of nineteen physicians, largely senior specialists at teaching medical colleges, independently reviewed every case and every one of the 224 grades. All seven production systems were evaluated through their public interfaces, and all 224 conversations are preserved as replayable links. Performance was poor across all systems, and the failures were shared: different vendors missed the same findings and converged on the same wrong plans. From the experts' notes we catalogue 18 recurring failure modes in five families. The models stop reading an image at the first finding. They give generic plans and lean toward over-treatment. They trust a misleading history over correct imaging. Their answers vary across systems and runs, and change with question format. Failing answers were delivered fluently and without any expressed uncertainty. Four cases are released in full; the remaining 28 are held out, and we invite frontier AI labs and healthcare AI companies to evaluate their models against them (research@futrbridge.com)

items.title: Co-DSL: Human-LLM Co-design of Reusable Spatial Concepts for Layout Generation
items.abstract: We present Co-DSL, a framework in which users and LLMs co-design reusable spatial concepts for layout generation. In the first stage, our system allows users to create a library of personalized operations. To add a concept, a user provides a description, which the LLM converts into an initial implementation. The user can then observe the concept's execution behavior over example scenarios and provide lightweight feedback to the LLM, which revises the concept's implementation logic. In the second stage, given a library, an LLM can author a layout program that meets a new layout request from a user. Executing a layout program instantiates a concept-graph, a declarative composition of library concepts. In this way, we require the LLM only to specify which concepts should hold, while we use a solver to search for a layout that satisfies them. Across five spatial layout domains, we find that Co-DSL libraries let LLMs capture layout patterns that are challenging for prior fixed-operation systems, and demonstrate that our concept-graph representation is needed for LLMs to reliably compose concepts together. We further find that Co-DSL lets LLMs author generative layout programs that expose high-level parametric controls users can manipulate to explore a distribution of related layouts without re-prompting.

items.title: Coarse-Grained Predictive Resource Allocation Framework enabling In-Premise XR Collaborations
items.abstract: Immersive extended reality (XR) applications are key enablers of human-centric connectivity in next-generation networks. However, meeting their high-throughput, ultra-low-latency, and high-reliability demands while preventing cyber-sickness remains a critical challenge, especially in environments with non-deterministic wireless connectivity. Fiber-To-The-Room (FTTR), extending widely deployed Fiber-To-The-Home (FTTH) infrastructure, offers a promising solution. Yet, satisfying the stringent Quality-of-Experience (QoE) requirements of XR collaborators demands robust resource allocation across the multi-tier cascade of FTTH, FTTR, and WiFi segments. In this paper, we propose a coarse-grained traffic forecasting-empowered proactive resource allocation and intelligent in-premise roaming framework. Here, artificial intelligence (AI) model complexities are scaled to the computational capabilities of each network segment. At the FTTR segment, we employ a hybrid temporal convolutional and bi-directional long short-term memory (TCN-BiLSTM) network for multi-modal XR traffic forecasting, integrating passive optical network (PON) and WiFi access points with multi-link operation (MLO) and orthogonal frequency-division multiple access (OFDMA). The resulting long-horizon forecasts reduce inference frequency, enabling coordinated FTTR-WiFi resource allocation and seamless network-orchestrated mobility across rooms. At the FTTH segment, we deploy Transformer-based time-series models (e.g., Informer, Autoformer, PatchTST, and TFT) to predict the complex XR traffic aggregated in FTTR segments for transmission over the FTTH backhaul. Evaluations show Transformer-based models are up to $\sim$75% more accurate in long-horizon forecasting than the hybrid model. Extensive simulations confirm the proposed framework significantly outperforms traditional methods in satisfying XR QoE requirements.

items.title: Compositional Performance Modeling of LLM Inference Clusters with Hierarchical KV Caching
items.abstract: Design-space exploration of LLM inference clusters requires predicting how hardware and serving policies interact with hierarchical key-value (KV) caching. Isolated operation profiles alone do not determine cluster latency: reuse changes computational demand, while KV location, capacity, and contention govern execution order. We present a compositional discrete-event simulator based on separating local service costs from shared resource and KV availability. Compute and transfer models calibrated on one-prefill/one-decode (1P-1D) deployments are reused across compatible workers, enabling policy and topology comparisons without per-configuration latency fitting. Validation against SGLang covers Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B on 1P-1D and 3P-1D clusters. Mean request end-to-end latency error is 1.34% for question answering and 6.36% for captured coding sessions, measured as mean absolute percentage error. CPU simulation reduces replay turnaround by 15.33 times on average; real replay includes prescribed arrival gaps. Measured session-affinity and simulated retention studies demonstrate how the framework guides policy selection by predicting the joint effects on computation, latency, and KV occupancy.

items.title: Consensus Embedding Geometry for Taxonomy Discovery in Psychological Domains
items.abstract: Psychological domains contain many constructs whose meanings are specified through natural-language definitions and examples. Organizing these vocabularies requires methods that connect semantic representations to interpretable categories and expose the effects of analytical choices. We present a researcher-guided framework combining construct prototypes, consensus similarity across embedding models, classical multidimensional scaling, and clustering in theory-guided feature spaces. Averaging model-specific cosine matrices produces a positive-semidefinite consensus kernel that accommodates different embedding dimensions. Global geometry supports broad organization, domain features support intermediate grouping, and local geometry supports finer subdivision. We demonstrate the framework on 224 abuse constructs represented by working definitions supplied by generative artificial intelligence and seven synthetic examples per construct. The resulting hierarchy distinguishes psychological domination from environmental violation and provides finer categories within each branch. Comparisons with single-model, definition-only, example-only, and direct-clustering alternatives identify the roles of representation and subdivision choices. The contribution is a reproducible workflow and stage-specific evaluation for exploratory taxonomy discovery. The case study establishes the dependence of its output on identifiable modeling choices, with category validity and cross-domain transfer remaining questions for further study.

items.title: Corpus-Adaptive Symptom Prototype Learning for Social-Media Depression Detection
items.abstract: Psychiatric-scale-guided screening has shown promise for social-media depression detection, but existing methods largely treat clinical symptom templates as fixed inputs and focus on improving screening or classification architectures. We instead investigate whether the symptom representation itself can be adapted to social-media language while retaining psychiatric priors. Fixed clinical templates exhibit three key mismatches with online expression: formal versus colloquial language, limited coverage of platform-specific signals, and linguistic distance that can weaken semantic matching. To address these mismatches, we propose Corpus-Adaptive Symptom Prototype Learning, which derives complementary symptom prototypes from depressed users’ training posts through semantic clustering and symptom extraction, refinement and deduplication, and social-media-style rewriting. The learned prototypes are combined with existing psychiatric templates and integrated in a plug-and-play manner without modifying downstream detection architectures. Experiments on eRisk2017 and eRisk2018 across five structurally diverse detection backbones show that the proposed representation consistently improves F1 and recall across all ten dataset–backbone combinations. Ablation results further show that the gains arise from corpus-derived symptom information rather than LLM-generated reformulations alone, and all three prototype-construction stages contribute to performance. These results demonstrate that adapting symptom representations, rather than only detection architectures, provides an effective and architecture-agnostic extension to psychiatric-scale-guided screening.

items.title: Dari mesin jawaban menjadi teman berpikir: Reorientasi peran artificial intelligence dalam pembelajaran mendalam di pendidikan tinggi
items.abstract: Perkembangan generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) telah mengubah cara mahasiswa memperoleh, mengolah, dan menghasilkan pengetahuan di pendidikan tinggi. Kemudahan memperoleh jawaban secara instan meningkatkan efisiensi pembelajaran, tetapi juga berpotensi mendorong cognitive offloading dan mengurangi keterlibatan mahasiswa dalam proses berpikir. Artikel ini bertujuan menganalisis pembelajaran mendalam (deep learning pedagogy) sebagai respons pedagogis terhadap disrupsi GenAI serta merumuskan reorientasi peran AI dari answer machine menjadi thinking partner. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan desain analisis konseptual melalui sintesis literatur ilmiah, teori, dan dokumen kebijakan mengenai GenAI, cognitive offloading, konstruktivisme, berpikir kritis, metakognisi, dan pembelajaran mendalam. Hasil sintesis menunjukkan bahwa persoalan utama penggunaan GenAI bukan keberadaan cognitive offloading, melainkan pendelegasian aktivitas kognitif yang menggantikan proses berpikir yang menjadi tujuan pembelajaran. Artikel ini merumuskan efficiency–depth paradox, yaitu ketegangan antara peningkatan efisiensi melalui AI dan kebutuhan untuk mempertahankan kedalaman proses belajar. Pembelajaran mendalam melalui prinsip mindful, meaningful, dan joyful learning dapat berfungsi sebagai pedagogical safeguards. Reorientasi AI sebagai thinking partner menempatkan mahasiswa sebagai primary thinker, sementara AI berfungsi sebagai scaffolding untuk questioning, exploration, feedback, verification, dan reflection.

items.title: Data-Based Exploration of Gold in Chartered Lands: Combining Remote Sensing and Artificial Intelligence in Hajjah Province, Yemen.
items.abstract: This study analyzes and collects data to assess gold exploration in uncharted sites of Hajjah province, Yemen, is predominantly caused by the time constraints, dangers, and limits of the exploration. The province is located in the Arabian-Nubian shield, which is an under explored site because of the unending logistical constraints and geopolitical issues. This study is the first to develop a framework for artificial intelligence-based and context-driven mineral prospect mapping for regional frontiers. Remote sensing data from ASTER and Sentinel-2 were used to establish zone maps for hydrothermal alteration (areas of historical geological change) and for various rock type indicators.This model used density and intersection analyses based on lineament density and digital elevation model (DEM) analyses. A mineral-system framework was modeled to provide various datasets with the random forest and data-efficient deep learning mechanisms, with special reference to the sparse deep forest architecture and the imbalanced dataset. The data and local conditions were adapted through transfer learning and data augmentation within physically defined limits. The findings support gold prospecting within the alteration-related and structurally controlled prospecting, which is consistent with the organic models. Prospecting maps based on probabilistic prospecting and metrics of uncertainty support the prospecting of target areas, which is consistent with the defined risks, and demonstrate for a smart exploration model for under explored terrains.

items.title: DBDM: a formal framework for bias detection and mitigation in distributed large language models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed in distributed settings, where different nodes may work on heterogeneous data, user populations, and local model updates. In such settings, bias can arise in an emergent fashion via local interactions and spread over the connected nodes, turning fairness into a property of the network rather than of the model. In this paper, we introduce Distributed Bias Detection and Mitigation (DBDM), a formal framework to model, detect, and mitigate dynamically evolving bias in distributed LLM settings. DBDM captures node-level bias in a multi-dimensional state consisting of statistical divergence, embedding disparity and response asymmetry, allowing bias to be monitored beyond a single output-level metric. The proposed framework combines local bias-aware optimisation with cross-node bias propagation modelling and graph-based consensus alignment, such that neighbouring nodes can coordinate fairness corrections while preserving the underlying distributed learning process. We evaluate the proposed framework through controlled distributed simulations with publicly available fairness benchmarks including StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs and BOLD. Experiments examine convergence, stability, scalability and multi-dimensional bias mitigation. Further, a real-transformer proof-of-concept experiment is performed on an open-access CrowS-Pairs subset with a lightweight PyTorch Transformer Encoder. In the pilot experiment, DBDM reduces the composite bias by ~ 48.5% and the inter-node bias-state variance by ~ 87.4% when compared to FedAvg over ten independent runs, while achieving statistically comparable fairness performance to FairFL. We also observe from communication analysis that explicitly communicating the bias state incurs a moderate additional communication overhead of around 8.3–8.8% over the conventional parameter aggregation for the configurations we experimented with. The results provide evidence that explicit modelling of bias states and consensus-based coordination can improve the fairness consistency of distributed learning systems at the network-level. The study also exposes practical challenges around communication latency, asynchronous participation, privacy protection, heterogeneous nodes, and production scale LLM validation which are important directions for future work.

items.title: Decision Reassessment Under Restricted Evidence Access
items.abstract: Incremental inference, provenance and conservative decision rules can support reassessment when underlying evidence changes but cannot be disclosed in full. This paper proposes a combined protocol for advisory records using recipient-authorized impact bounds, explicit dependencies and auditable issuance states. The contribution is a testable integration specification and comparative evaluation plan, not new mathematics or a deployed capability. Synthetic fixtures check selected rule behavior; they do not establish intelligence accuracy or operational benefit. A proposed six-month feasibility study would compare cost, decision coverage, disclosure and analyst burden against equally informed conventional implementations. No comparative pilot, government deployment, security accreditation, operational validation or quantum advantage is reported. Independent decision-science, security, legal, privacy and human-factors review remains necessary. items.title: Decision Theory and Artificial Intelligence: An Anatomical Review of Output Contracts, Acquisition Geometries, and Epistemic Verticals
items.abstract: This paper presents a detailed anatomical review of Miquel Noguer i Alonso's "Decision Theory and Artificial Intelligence" (2026). The reviewed work develops a unified Bayesian decision-theoretic framework that links feasible action spaces, reward functions, statistical estimation targets, and costly information acquisition policies. Central contributions include minimal output contracts for specified reward families (Theorem 4.5), regret propagation decompositions (Proposition 6.1), capacity-constrained optimal gates with complementary slackness (Theorem 7.1), an acquisition-output contract characterising compressed representations that preserve nonnegative-price routing decisions (Theorem 7.6), and a routing-geometry dichotomy between discrete decisions (information most valuable near action boundaries) and continuous quadratic sizing (precision gains favouring strongest signals) (Proposition 7.13). The framework accommodates supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, large language models, and typed probability interfaces such as JEV. A retrospective empirical study of 27,241 LLM cases evaluates cost-aware replacement routing. This review systematically examines the paper's strengths and limitations, situates it against at least ten competing models and theories in decision theory, statistical treatment rules, cascade deferral, metareasoning, and decision-focused learning, and articulates the ontological and epistemological verticals underlying the evolution of its central themes. Possible extensions and ideation pathways are proposed. All references follow Harvard style. KSCCN review article, 11 October 2026. Dr. Syed Muntasir Mamun, ORCID 0000-0001-6845-2853. The views expressed are those of the author.

items.title: Decomposition-Induced Governance Blindness: Assurance continuity across decomposed governance systems
items.abstract: Complex organisations become governable by decomposition. Responsibilities are distributed among specialist functions, committees, professions, programmes and assurance regimes so that bounded attention and expertise can be applied to manageable parts of a larger system. Yet consequential relationships do not necessarily share those jurisdictional boundaries. A proposition about service recoverability, digital benefit, transformation resilience or organisational performance may depend on conditions governed by several domains even when every domain performs its local role competently. This paper develops Decomposition-Induced Governance Blindness (DIGB) as a candidate construct for the resulting loss of assurance continuity. DIGB is defined as the loss or degradation of current whole-system assurance over consequential relationships, dependencies or propositions that cross the jurisdictions into which governance has been decomposed. It is theorised to arise where such crossings lack mechanisms that preserve their visibility, ownership and validity across domains and over time. The paper introduces the Cross-Domain Governance Object (CDGO) as the principal unit of analysis: a consequential relationship, proposition, dependency or state whose validity depends on conditions governed across two or more domains, so that its assurance may not follow from assurance of its constituent components. Governance Architecture Misalignment (GAM) is specified as an antecedent, and compensating mechanisms are modelled separately as suppressors. DIGB is observed through outcomes coded independently of those mechanisms: detection latency, persistence of unsupported propositions, and consequential decisions made while such propositions are relied upon. Visibility loss, ownership discontinuity and assurance discontinuity are treated as candidate explanatory processes. The paper distinguishes DIGB from near-decomposability, interdependence, mirroring, coordination neglect, structural secrecy, incubation and drift, silos, boundary spanning, structural holes, the problem of many hands, systems safety, high-reliability organising, combined and dynamic assurance, business continuity and operational resilience. A structured comparison with these rivals, summarised in Table 1, finds that each explains part of the phenomenon. Dynamic assurance cases maintain such propositions where they have been constituted as assurance objects; DIGB concerns consequential cross-domain propositions that lack that coverage and explains why decomposed governance leaves them uncovered. Five falsifiable propositions are advanced. The central theoretical claim is that whole-system assurance depends not only on assurance quality within domains but on whether consequential relationships crossing those domains are themselves objects of continuing assurance. Four independently developed methods — Structural Decision Intelligence, the Digital Transformation Resilience Model, a business-continuity and operational-resilience application of DTRM, and a Digital Value Realisation Framework — are used as theory-motivating material rather than validation. Their recurrence motivates a spatial and temporal account of governance blindness: an organisation can retain competent local governance, adequate information, clear functional accountability and historically valid assurance while losing current assurance of the whole-system proposition. A staged empirical programme is specified to test whether DIGB adds explanatory and detection value beyond established theories. items.title: Delegation Is Not Assistance: Agentic AI and Assessment Governance in Higher Education - A Comparative Documentary Analysis of 12 Universities
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) assessment policies in higher education have centred on originality, disclosure, and permission to use AI. Agentic AI, which can plan, use tools, access platforms, and act with limited human intervention, challenges this logic because it can take over the whole action chain of an assessed task rather than only generate content. This study examines how assessment governance changes from GenAI to agentic AI. Using exploratory comparative documentary analysis, public central guidance from 12 universities was theoretically sampled: six agentic-aware cases and six GenAI-dominant comparators, with a retrieval cut-off of 3 October 2026. Documents were coded on six dimensions using a directed framework informed by Bacchi’s “What’s the Problem Represented to Be?” approach. All agentic-aware cases distinguished agentic AI from GenAI, and most set explicit delegation and access boundaries, whereas no comparator explicitly addressed agents operating institutional systems on a student’s behalf. The comparators, however, were strong on evidence of learning and task-level transparency, and programme-level assurance was sparse in both groups. The study proposes the Delegation-Evidence-Access (DEA) framework, which moves governance from tool permission towards responsibility allocation, and derives four assessment contexts and a task-, course-, and programme-level implementation model. Implications for Malaysian higher education are discussed. Findings are descriptive, based on selected public documents, and not representative; no inter-rater reliability was assessed.

items.title: Dermoscopy at an Inflection Point: Sharper Criteria, New Optics, and the Arrival of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Dermoscopy improves the diagnosis of melanoma and keratinocyte carcinoma, but its value depends on the observer, the lesion mix, the anatomic site, and the action taken after the examination. Recent reviews have mainly focused on one modality or image-classification accuracy. This narrative review follows the clinical pathway and compares five linked areas: defined diagnostic criteria, sequential digital monitoring, site- and skin-tone-specific interpretation, multimodal imaging, and artificial intelligence (AI). Melanoma and keratinocyte carcinoma are discussed separately because their criteria, diagnostic problems, imaging needs, and management differ. Meta-analyses support dermoscopy over naked-eye examination, although accuracy remains closely related to clinician experience. A randomized trial of three-dimensional total-body photography with sequential dermoscopy led to more procedures and higher costs without finding more malignant tumors over two years. Reflectance confocal microscopy can improve specificity in selected equivocal lesions, while optical coherence technologies add architectural and depth information that is most relevant to keratinocyte carcinoma. AI has moved from retrospective benchmarks to prospective multicenter studies, but false-positive burden, dataset shift, underrepresentation of darker skin tones, limited explainability, and uncertain workflow effects remain. The review also considers foundation models, regulation, and patient-facing tools and uses a SWOT analysis to define research priorities. The field is at an inflection point in evidence, not image quality. Progress should be judged by effects on biopsy decisions, missed-cancer rates, timeliness, cost, access, and patient outcomes in defined populations.

items.title: DIGITAL INTELLIGENCE, ETHICAL AI GOVERNANCE, AND HUMAN INTELLIGENCE: A CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK FOR RESPONSIBLE DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN ASIAN COUNTRIES
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), big data analytics, and cloud computing are accelerating digital transformation by improving organizational efficiency, innovation, and data-driven decision-making across Asian economies. While these technologies create significant opportunities for economic and social development, they also introduce complex ethical challenges, including concerns related to privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, accountability, cybersecurity, and responsible governance. This conceptual paper proposes a human-centred framework that integrates digital intelligence, ethical AI governance, and human intelligence to support responsible digital transformation. Grounded in the resource-based view, dynamic capability theory, stakeholder theory, institutional theory, and socio-technical systems theory, the framework explains how technological capabilities, ethical governance mechanisms, and human competencies collectively contribute to sustainable organizational performance. This paper emphasises that ethical decision-making, creativity, critical thinking, and responsible leadership remain essential complements to AI-driven systems. By presenting an integrated conceptual perspective, this study offers theoretical insights for future research and practical guidance for policymakers, organizational leaders, and technology practitioners seeking to balance digital innovation with ethical responsibility and long-term societal well-being.

items.title: Digital Risks and AI-Enabled Responses in Adolescent Mental Health: A Bibliometric and Science-Mapping Analysis
items.abstract: Objective: This study mapped digital risks and AI-enabled responses in adolescent mental health, quantified publication balance, and tested explicit domain integration within single records. Method: Scopus metadata (frozen August 9, 2026; exported August 15, 2026) covering articles, reviews, and conference papers were analyzed via bibliometric mapping. Temporal trends evaluated 2015–2025 (complete years), reporting 2026 provisionally. Records were classified as Risk-only, Response-only, or Both. Robustness checks included audits, manual validation of Both records, sensitivity analyses, VOSviewer mapping, thematic evolution, burst detection, and network validation. Results: Of 4,804 retrieved records, 1,623 formed the primary corpus (1,335 in 2015–2025: 833 Risk-only, 495 Response-only, 7 Both). The response-to-risk ratio rose from 0.04 (2015) to 1.19 (2025), when response output first surpassed risk. Manual review confirmed only 5 direct bridges in 2015–2025 (0.37%) and 9 overall (0.55%); integration remained <1% across sensitivity analyses. Keyword mapping revealed distinct cyberbullying/victimization, AI/digital-mental-health, and machine-learning/suicide-prediction clusters, with recent growth in AI, digital phenotyping, and LLMs. Conclusion: Although AI response research has expanded rapidly, explicit co-framing of digital risk and AI response within single publications remains rare and independent of 2026 data.

items.title: Distilling Transitional Patterns to Multimodal Large Language Models for Session-based Recommendation
items.abstract: Session-based recommendation (SBR) predicts the next item based on anonymous sessions. Traditional SBR explores user intents based on ID collaborations or auxiliary content. To further alleviate data sparsity and cold-start issues, recent Multimodal SBR (MSBR) methods utilize simplistic pre-trained models for modality learning but have limitations in semantic richness. Considering the semantic reasoning abilities of multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) and the practical request for high inference efficiency, we focus on the LLM-enhanced MSBR scenario in this paper, which leverages LLM cognition for comprehensive multimodal representation generation, to enhance downstream MSBR. Tackling this problem faces two challenges: i) how to obtain LLM cognition on both inherent multimodal knowledge and transitional patterns, ii) how to align transitional patterns and inherent knowledge into one unified LLM without increasing inference complexity. To this end, we propose a multimodal LLM-enhanced framework TPAD, which extends a teacher-student distillation paradigm to decouple and align transitional patterns for promoting MSBR. TPAD establishes parallel Knowledge-MLLM and Transfer-MLLM, where the former as student model interprets item knowledge-reflected features and the latter as teacher model extracts transition-aware features. Transitional pattern alignment harnessing mutual information estimation unites two MLLMs, distilling transitional patterns into representations. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of TPAD. Implementation codes are available at https://github.com/TiliaceaeSU/TPAD .

items.title: Do LLM Tutors Actually Teach? A Process-Centered Synthesis of the Tutoring Loop
items.abstract: Large language models can produce fluent tu- toring dialogue, but whether they actually help students learn remains unclear. We present a process-centered synthesis of LLM tutoring that follows the path from learner-state infer- ence to pedagogical action, tutor training, eval- uation, and student simulation. This view ex- poses a central gap: implementing a tutoring component does not establish that it works or that its outputs meaningfully affect later stages. A structured study-level audit shows that peda- gogical evaluation is common, while evidence becomes much thinner for learner-conditioned intervention, human learning gains, and espe- cially transfer or delayed retention. Human studies nevertheless provide a conditional posi- tive result: LLM tutors can improve learning, but benefits depend on pedagogical structure, learner engagement, and how learning is mea- sured. We argue that progress requires validat- ing the interfaces between tutoring stages, not only improving individual components.

items.title: Effects of AI-Supported Learning on Independent Cognitive Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Instructional Scaffolding and Learner Characteristics
items.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis will examine the effects of AI-supported learning on objectively assessed cognitive performance when AI assistance is unavailable during assessment. It will cover intelligent tutoring systems, traditional chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and generative AI across educational stages and subject areas. Technology characteristics and instructional support functions will be coded separately, allowing overlapping features rather than imposing mutually exclusive technology categories. The primary objective is to estimate the effects of AI-supported learning compared with non-AI learning conditions on independent cognitive performance. Secondary objectives are to examine direct comparisons between AI-supported instructional approaches and whether effects vary with baseline learner characteristics and instructional support functions. Relevant support functions include hints, explanations, feedback, worked examples, self-explanation prompts, verification and revision prompts, adaptive learning pathways, and restrictions or fading of AI assistance. Randomized and non-randomized controlled intervention studies will be synthesized separately. A distinct observational evidence stream will examine associations between actual AI use, such as usage frequency, help-seeking, and verification behaviors, and eligible cognitive outcomes. These associations will not be combined with intervention effects or interpreted as causal evidence that a particular use behavior improves learning. Eligible outcomes include objective measures of knowledge and understanding, application and transfer, other cognitive skills, and composite achievement, which will be analyzed separately. The first eligible post-intervention assessment and subsequent delayed assessments will be distinguished. Assessments must be completed without AI; access to non-AI resources will be recorded separately. Unclear AI permissions will remain awaiting clarification rather than being treated as confirmed eligibility or grounds for automatic exclusion. Two human reviewers will independently screen records, extract key study information, and assess risk of bias, with disagreements reconciled. Analyses will account for overlapping reports, shared samples, dependent effect sizes, and differences in study design and comparison conditions. Moderator analyses will depend on sufficient comparable evidence. Within-study learner moderation will be distinguished from between-study associations. The review aims to clarify whether benefits of AI-supported learning persist when learners are assessed without AI, and which learner characteristics and instructional support functions may be associated with those benefits. No uniformly positive effect or ranking of technologies is assumed. Before registration, preliminary scoping and pilot screening examined 30 purposively selected candidate reports, and selected results from four reports underwent trial extraction to assess feasibility and refine the protocol. This prior exposure to study findings is disclosed. A comprehensive systematic database search, formal independent duplicate screening, complete data extraction, and quantitative synthesis have not yet been conducted. Substantive subsequent changes will be documented through dated amendments.

items.title: Enhancing network science with large language models and federated artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract Sixth generation (6G) networks require intelligent and privacy-preserving solutions to handle traffic complexity, resource allocation, and security challenges. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer advanced reasoning and Federated Artificial Intelligence (FAI) enables distributed learning without directly sharing raw data, their combined application in large-scale network science remains limited. Key issues include non-IID data, decision latency, and limited robustness of centralized models. To address these challenges, this work introduces FALCON-6G (Federated AI and LLM-Oriented Cognitive Optimization in 6G Networks), a novel framework for distributed anomaly detection, traffic prediction, and adaptive resource management. Experiments conducted under federated learning settings with 50 participating clients and 200 global communication rounds on two Open RAN and four intrusion detection datasets show a 22.7% average relative improvement in throughput prediction accuracy and a 17.6% reduction in decision latency compared with FedAvg, along with up to a 23.9% relative improvement in intrusion detection F1-score over FedAvg and a 34.0% reduction in communication overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of FALCON-6G for privacy-aware 6G network optimization. The current evaluation is primarily based on benchmark datasets, and validation in live large-scale 6G/O-RAN environments remains an important direction for future work.

items.title: ETSAM: effectively segmenting cell membranes in cryo-electron tomograms
items.abstract: Cryogenic Electron Tomography (cryo-ET) is an emerging experimental technique used to visualize cell structures and macromolecules in their native cellular environment. Accurate segmentation of cell structures in cryo-ET tomograms, such as cell membranes, supports the study of cellular organization and function. However, several inherent limitations in cryo-ET, including the very low signal-to-noise ratio, missing wedge artifacts from limited tilt angles, and other noise artifacts, collectively hinder the reliable identification and delineation of these structures. In this study, we present ETSAM, a two-stage Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2)-based fine-tuned AI method that effectively segments cell membranes in tomograms. It is trained on a diverse dataset comprising 83 experimental tomograms from the CryoET Data Portal (CDP) database and 28 simulated tomograms generated using PolNet. On an independent test set of 17 experimental tomograms for which ground-truth annotations are available, ETSAM outperforms other deep learning based methods by robustly identifying cell membranes with high sensitivity while also maintaining better precision. Cell membranes are hard to distinguish in the noisy 3D volumes from cryo-electron tomography. Here, authors adapt a video segmentation foundation model to the task, segmenting membranes across diverse organisms more accurately than existing tools.

items.title: Every Public Servant Was Once a student: Reimagining Education for Ethical Leadership, Public Service and Good Governance in Fiji and the Pacific
items.abstract: Not every student will become a public servant, but every public servant was once a student. This simple proposition raises a significant but insufficiently examined question about the wider purpose of education: to what extent does education contribute to forming the values, ethical judgement, critical consciousness and sense of public responsibility of those who later serve within public institutions? While education is frequently evaluated through academic achievement, qualifications, employability and economic productivity, comparatively less attention is given to its longer-term contribution to ethical public service and good governance. This conceptual paper critically examines the relationship between education, public-service formation and governance, with particular attention to Fiji and the wider Pacific. Drawing upon literature on democratic education, critical pedagogy, character and values education, the Capability Approach, public-service ethics and Indigenous Pacific epistemologies, the paper argues that the foundations of ethical public service begin long before an individual enters government employment. Schools, tertiary institutions, families and communities contribute to developing integrity, responsibility, empathy, critical thinking, cultural understanding, respect for diversity and commitment to the public good. These capabilities become increasingly important as public servants confront complex challenges involving inequality, climate change, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, cultural diversity and declining or contested public trust. The paper proposes an Education–Public Service–Society Cycle to conceptualise the intergenerational relationship through which education contributes to professional and civic formation; public servants subsequently influence policy implementation, institutional integrity and service delivery; and the quality of public institutions, in turn, shapes the educational and social opportunities available to future generations. In the Fiji and Pacific context, the paper further argues that ethical public-service formation should integrate professional competence with Indigenous values of relationality, collective responsibility, service and cultural accountability. It concludes that education should not merely prepare people to obtain employment in public institutions, but contribute to developing people capable of serving the public ethically, competently, equitably and with humanity. Reimagining education in this way positions the classroom as one of the earliest foundations of trustworthy institutions, responsible public administration and sustainable Pacific futures.

items.title: Exploring artificial intelligence usage preferences among medical students in Iran: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into medical education, offering opportunities to enhance learning, research, and clinical preparation. Although previous studies have explored medical students’ attitudes and acceptance of AI, evidence regarding their AI usage preferences remains limited, particularly in developing countries where AI integration into medical education is still evolving. Understanding these preferences is essential for designing context-appropriate educational strategies and responsible AI integration. This study aimed to examine the preferences and patterns of AI usage among students at Shiraz University of Medical Sciences (SUMS), Iran. This descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted in 2025 among undergraduate and postgraduate students at SUMS. Using stratified random sampling, 384 students were recruited. Data were collected between July and October 2025 using a validated self-administered questionnaire (AI-UPSS; Cronbach’s α = 0.935), assessing AI usage across eight domains. Responses were rated on a 4-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed using one-sample t-tests, independent t-tests, and one-way ANOVA in SPSS version 24, with a cutoff mean score of 2.5. The highest mean preference scores were observed in Research & Writing (Mean = 2.66 ± 0.79, p < 0.001) and Self-learning/Education (Mean = 2.61 ± 0.81, p = 0.010). Moderate preferences were found for Curiosity & Entertainment (Mean = 2.36 ± 0.81, p = 0.001) and Health Counseling (Mean = 2.40 ± 0.96, p = 0.044). The lowest scores were reported in Design & Programming (Mean = 1.54 ± 0.79, p < 0.001) and Art (Mean = 1.68 ± 0.77, p < 0.001). Significant gender differences were observed in Art ( p = 0.010), Self-learning ( p = 0.027), and Health Counseling ( p < 0.001). GPA was significantly associated with Content Development ( p = 0.004), Design & Programming ( p = 0.031), and Art ( p = 0.032), with higher usage among students with lower GPAs. Undergraduate students showed significantly higher preferences across several domains, including curiosity and health counseling ( p < 0.01). Medical students primarily use AI for academic, research, and self-directed learning purposes, while engagement with technical and creative applications remains limited. AI usage preferences are influenced by academic level, gender, and GPA rather than age or field of study. These findings underscore the need for structured, level-specific AI education to promote effective and ethical AI integration in medical curricula.

items.title: Factors Associated With Low Back Pain Complaints Among Warehouse Workers At PT. X In 2026
items.abstract: Low Back Pain (LBP) is one of the most common musculoskeletal disorders experienced by warehouse workers due to manual handling activities, non-ergonomic working postures, and repetitive physical workloads. This condition may reduce work productivity and negatively affect workers' health. This study aimed to determine the factors associated with Low Back Pain complaints among warehouse workers at PT. X in 2026. This quantitative study employed a cross-sectional design. The study population consisted of 81 warehouse workers, all of whom were included as the research sample using a total sampling technique. Data were collected using the Nordic Body Map (NBM) questionnaire to identify Low Back Pain complaints, while working posture was assessed using the Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) method. Data were analyzed using univariate and bivariate analyses with the Chi-Square test at a 95% confidence level (α = 0.05). The findings indicated that most warehouse workers experienced Low Back Pain complaints. Bivariate analysis showed that age and length of employment were significantly associated with Low Back Pain complaints (p < 0.05), whereas working duration was not significantly associated with Low Back Pain (p > 0.05). The REBA assessment revealed that most work activities were classified as having moderate to high ergonomic risk, indicating the need for corrective ergonomic interventions. It can be concluded that age and length of employment are factors associated with Low Back Pain complaints among warehouse workers at PT. X. The company is recommended to implement ergonomic programs, provide manual handling aids, and conduct regular ergonomic training and working posture evaluations to reduce the risk of Low Back Pain.

items.title: FAIR Research Data Management with NOMAD and FAIRmat
items.abstract: These slides accompanied an invited tutorial presented at TCO 2026 on 28 September 2026 in Leipzig, Germany. The presentation introduces NOMAD, a free, open-source research data management platform developed and operated by FAIRmat, a consortium of the German National Research Data Infrastructure (NFDI). NOMAD enables researchers to upload, organize, explore, analyze, and publish their data. By transforming heterogeneous research data into structured, machine-readable formats, the platform helps make them findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR). The presentation provides an overview of relevant concepts, tools, and practical workflows for managing materials-science data throughout the research lifecycle. It covers data upload and automated processing, metadata extraction and enrichment, schema-based data modelling, data organization, search and exploration, analysis, and publication. It also introduces NOMAD’s support for experimental and computational data and discusses how structured, contextualized datasets can be prepared for machine-learning and artificial-intelligence applications. Both NOMAD deployment options are presented: the publicly accessible central platform and NOMAD Oasis, a customizable infrastructure that research groups and institutions can host and operate independently. The slides are intended for researchers, developers, and research-data professionals interested in interoperable data infrastructures, reproducible research, and applying the FAIR principles to computational and experimental materials science.

items.title: Fairy tales to fairer tales: Generative AI-supported critical multimodal literacy in pre-service preschool teacher education
items.abstract: This study investigates how pre-service teachers can use generative artificial intelligence (AI) to retell classic fairy tales in a way that challenges the biases that they frequently contain. A qualitative action research study involving 60 pre-service preschool teachers (46 female and 14 male) was carried out at a public university in Türkiye. Data collection included video recordings of instructional sessions (4 weeks, two lesson hours per week), participants’ fairer tales, and field notes. Drawing on the Critical Multimodal Literacy (CML) framework, the participants used generative AI tools to iteratively reimagine the textual and visual elements of traditional fairy tales. 11 reimagined fairy tales were analyzed under three themes: challenging traditional power dynamics, critiquing societal norms, and promoting non-violent conflict resolution. The findings indicate that the participants engaged in CLM by restructuring dominant representations of gender, identity, and conflict through the use of textual and visual modes. While generative AI supported the production of multimodal texts, participants maintained their agency through processes of prompting, evaluating, redesigning, and revising the outputs, emphasizing AI’s role as a mediational tool rather than an autonomous creator. The findings suggest that AI-supported fairy tale rewriting may provide a pedagogical context that enables pre-service preschool teachers to produce alternative representations of equality and social justice for children.

items.title: Fast and Accurate: Improving Personalized LLM Performance by Semantic Concentration Inspired Workload Split between RAG and Fine-Tuning
items.abstract: With ever increasing personalized large language model (LLM) services, the next question to answer is how to improve the quality of services/users' experiences, which is indicated by personalized LLM generation accuracy/quality and inference latency. Although state-of-the-art designs, e.g., parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or Full PEFT+RAG, can help, they largely ignore the heterogeneous semantic concentrations of users' historical data and cannot fully unleash the potential of personal data for personalized LLM performance enhancement. In this paper, we propose PEFT Union RAG (PUR), a novel ``fast and accurate'' approach that exploits the semantic concentration of users' personal historical data to split workload between PEFT and RAG, aiming to improve personalized LLM performance in terms of better generation accuracy/quality and lower inference latency. Briefly, PUR partitions user's personal historical data and assigns semantic concentrated ``core'' information to PEFT for offline parametric fine-tuning, while retaining dispersed information for RAG. During the online LLM inference, PUR directly generates responses for ``core'' queries covered by the PEFT region and invokes RAG only for sporadic ``peripheral'' queries. Experimental results show that, by appropriately splitting workload between PEFT and RAG, PUR consistently achieves the best generation accuracy/quality for various users across multiple tasks, while reducing inference latency by 14.4%--46.6% compared with the best performed method.
